title: Session-vs-token separation: Keycloak owns tokens; the project may issue an app session on top
description: Keycloak is the token authority: it mints the access token, the id_token, and the refresh token; the browser never holds a project-minted JWT and the browser never holds a Keycloak refresh token. The project MAY layer an application session on top of the verified token stream: the reference wiring issues an opaque-handle session cookie whose server-side record stores the Keycloak-minted tokens keyed by the handle (mirroring the vendor-neutral sibling's opaque-handle posture, and following the composition pattern where the session-record store injects). The alternate posture the operator MAY declare is `sessionMode: 'stateless'` on the realm record, in which case no server-side session record is kept and every request re-verifies the access token from a bearer header (or a cookie carrying the token verbatim, per the operator's declared bearer source). The two postures are not composable per realm record; the operator picks one. The reduced Principal (`principalId`, `provider`, `email?`, `roles[]`, `organisationIds[]`) is the only claim shape the project's own handlers ever see; provider tokens are inaccessible from `request.auth` in both modes.
rationale: Keycloak's authority over token issuance is a vendor commitment; the blueprint's authority is over what the project builds around that stream. Two postures serve two operator populations: a stateful session-record wiring (the reference default) matches small projects that want a single opaque cookie and cheap sign-out, and a stateless bearer posture matches deployments where the project can accept per-request verification cost and wants to avoid a session store. Both postures gate provider tokens behind the mechanism boundary so no handler code path reads a Keycloak-minted token directly.
